notes.front: What is the Prometheus server, as the Overview describes it among the ecosystem's components?
notes.back: The main component which scrapes and stores time series data — the core of the Prometheus ecosystem.
notes.explanation: The Overview lists it first among the ecosystem’s components, many of which are optional.
notes.example: Like a warehouse that receives goods and holds them in stock, while other buildings feed it or act on what it holds.

notes.front: What is a target, in Prometheus?
notes.back: The definition of an object to scrape — for example, what labels to apply, any required authentication, or other scrape settings.
notes.explanation: A target is the configuration Prometheus needs before it can scrape somewhere, not just the endpoint's raw address.
notes.example: Like an entry in a delivery round: not just an address, but the gate code and any other instructions the driver needs.

notes.front: What is a scrape, in Prometheus?
notes.back: One HTTP fetch of a target's metrics, made under the parameters a scrape_config describes for that target.
notes.explanation: A scrape_config “specifies a set of targets and parameters describing how to scrape them” — the scrape is that fetch itself.
notes.example: Like one round a postal courier makes to a single house: one visit, one collection.

notes.front: In Prometheus terms, what is an instance?
notes.back: An endpoint you can scrape, usually corresponding to a single process.
notes.explanation: It's one member of a job: the docs' own api-server example lists four separate instances, one per replica.
notes.example: Like one till in a shop with four tills all doing the same job: each till is its own instance.

notes.front: In Prometheus terms, what is a job?
notes.back: A collection of instances with the same purpose, such as a process replicated for scalability or reliability.
notes.explanation: The four-replica api-server example in the docs is one job made up of four instances.
notes.example: Like a shift of four cashiers all doing the same role: the shift is the job, each cashier is an instance.

notes.front: What is Prometheus's local TSDB (time series database)?
notes.back: The local time series database that stores scraped data in a custom, highly efficient on-disk format.
notes.explanation: It's what “Local storage” in the docs refers to: data written to disk in Prometheus's own block format, not a generic database.
notes.example: Like a specialised filing cabinet built for just one kind of paperwork, rather than a general-purpose filing system.

notes.front: What should a Prometheus metric name specify, according to the data model?
notes.back: The general feature of a system being measured, such as http_requests_total for the total number of HTTP requests received.
notes.explanation: That naming habit is what makes a metric name readable on its own, before any labels are attached.
notes.example: Like naming a spreadsheet column “monthly_sales_total” rather than just “value” — the name alone says what's inside.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Data model, “Metric names and labels”

notes.front: In Prometheus's data model, what do labels let you do with a metric name?
notes.back: Capture different instances of the same metric name — for example, splitting HTTP requests by method and handler.
notes.explanation: This is what the docs call Prometheus's “dimensional data model”: labels add filterable, aggregatable dimensions to one metric name.
notes.example: Like tagging photos by “location” and “year”: the same “photo” metric splits into filterable dimensions.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Data model, “Metric names and labels”

notes.front: What is a sample, in a Prometheus time series?
notes.back: A single value at a point in time — a float64 value with a millisecond-precision timestamp.
notes.explanation: A time series is just an ordered stream of these individual samples, one value per timestamp.
notes.example: Like one entry in a temperature log: one reading, one exact time it was taken.

notes.front: What is a Prometheus counter?
notes.back: A cumulative metric whose value can only increase, or be reset to zero on restart.
notes.explanation: That's why counters suit things like request or error totals: values that only ever grow between resets.
notes.example: Like a car's odometer: it only climbs, and only resets if something restarts it from zero.

notes.front: What is a Prometheus gauge?
notes.back: A metric representing a single numerical value that can arbitrarily go up and down.
notes.explanation: Temperatures, current memory usage and concurrent-request counts are all examples the docs give of values that move in both directions.
notes.example: Like a car's fuel gauge: it rises when you refuel and falls as you drive, moving freely in either direction.

notes.front: What is a Prometheus histogram?
notes.back: A metric that records observations by counting them into configurable buckets, and also provides a sum of all observed values.
notes.explanation: That's why the docs call it “essentially a bucketed counter”: each bucket counts observations at or below its bound.
notes.example: Like sorting parcels into weight bands, while also keeping a running total of all the weights combined.

notes.front: What is a Prometheus summary?
notes.back: A metric that samples observations like a histogram, but calculates configurable quantiles over a sliding time window.
notes.explanation: Where a histogram exposes bucket counts and leaves the quantile to the server, a summary calculates its quantiles inside the instrumented program itself.
notes.example: Like a shop tracking not just how many sales happened, but its own running estimate of the median sale value.

notes.front: What exposition format must processes use, by default, to expose metrics to Prometheus?
notes.back: The Prometheus text exposition format — a line-oriented, human-readable text format.
notes.explanation: It has been the default since Prometheus 2.0; the protobuf format is only used behind HTTP content negotiation.
notes.example: Like a shop receipt printed in plain text rather than a barcode: readable on its own, without special equipment.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Exposition formats, “Prometheus Text Format”

notes.front: What is OpenMetrics?
notes.back: An effort to standardise metric wire formatting, built off of the Prometheus text format.
notes.explanation: Prometheus can both scrape OpenMetrics targets and use it for federating metrics.
notes.example: Like an industry-standard shipping label built from one company's own label design, so other companies can read it too.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Exposition formats, “OpenMetrics Text Format”

notes.front: What does an exemplar provide, in the OpenMetrics format?
notes.back: A point-in-time snapshot related to an otherwise summarised metric, which may also carry a trace ID.
notes.explanation: That optional trace ID is what can link a summarised metric value back to one specific traced request.
notes.example: Like a single receipt kept alongside a shop's total daily takings: one concrete example behind an otherwise summarised number.

notes.front: What is the Prometheus protobuf format?
notes.back: An officially supported binary exposition format, used alongside the text-based formats.
notes.explanation: The docs list forward/backward compatibility and support for streaming large scrapes among its advantages over text.
notes.example: Like sending a parcel's contents as a compact packing manifest instead of a handwritten letter: less readable, but more efficient.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Exposition formats, “Prometheus Protobuf Format”

notes.front: What is relabeling, in Prometheus configuration?
notes.back: A tool to dynamically rewrite a target's label set before it gets scraped.
notes.explanation: It runs as ordered steps, each one applied to the label set the steps before it produced.
notes.example: Like editing a parcel's shipping label before it leaves the depot, so it's addressed correctly by the time it's picked up.

notes.front: What is remote write, in Prometheus?
notes.back: A feature that sends ingested samples on the fly to other systems, such as long-term storage.
notes.explanation: Local storage alone doesn't scale beyond one node, so remote write is how Prometheus hands data off to something that can.
notes.example: Like a shop wiring its daily takings straight to the bank as they come in, rather than only keeping cash in the till.

notes.front: What is remote read, in Prometheus?
notes.back: A feature that lets Prometheus transparently read time series from other systems, such as long-term storage, as part of a query.
notes.explanation: It's the reverse direction from remote write: a query pulls older or external data back in, rather than pushing samples out.
notes.example: Like a shop pulling archived sales records back from a warehouse to answer a query about last year's takings.

notes.front: What does federation allow one Prometheus server to do?
notes.back: Scrape selected time series from another Prometheus server.
notes.explanation: It reuses the ordinary scrape mechanism, just pointed at another Prometheus server's /federate endpoint instead of an application.
notes.example: Like one branch office pulling a summary of figures from another branch's own records, rather than collecting the raw data itself.

notes.front: In the Prometheus architecture diagram, how does Prometheus reach a short-lived job's metrics that could vanish before a scrape?
notes.back: Via an intermediary push gateway, which the short-lived job pushes to and Prometheus then scrapes.
notes.explanation: The Overview says Prometheus “scrapes metrics from instrumented jobs, either directly or via an intermediary push gateway for short-lived jobs.”

image.alt: The Prometheus architecture diagram: service discovery (such as file_sd) supplies targets; the Prometheus server pulls metrics from jobs and exporters, and from a Pushgateway that short-lived jobs push to when they exit; it stores data in its TSDB on local disk, pushes alerts to the Alertmanager, which notifies email, pager and chat services, and is queried with PromQL by its web UI, Grafana and other API clients.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from the Prometheus documentation, Overview (architecture diagram)

notes.front: Besides the Prometheus server itself, what are two other components the Overview lists in the Prometheus ecosystem?
notes.back: Any two of: client libraries, a push gateway, special-purpose exporters, an Alertmanager, or various support tools.
notes.explanation: The Overview says many of these components are optional, and calls the Prometheus server the main one.

notes.front: Does the Overview say that every component of the Prometheus ecosystem is needed in every setup?
notes.back: No. It says the ecosystem consists of multiple components, “many of which are optional”.
notes.explanation: The Overview doesn’t say which components are optional; it calls the Prometheus server the main component, which scrapes and stores time series data.

notes.front: When Prometheus scrapes a target, it automatically attaches a {{c1::job}} label (the configured job name) and an instance label (the host:port scraped).
notes.explanation: These two labels are what let a scraped series be traced back to the job and instance it came from, even before any relabeling.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Jobs and instances, “Automatically generated labels and time series”

notes.front: A scraped target already exposes its own “job” label in its metrics, which conflicts with the job label Prometheus would attach automatically. What decides how that conflict is resolved?
notes.back: The honor_labels configuration option, set on that target's scrape configuration.
notes.explanation: The jobs and instances page points to honor_labels for exactly this case: it governs what happens when scraped data and Prometheus's own labels collide.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Jobs and instances, “Automatically generated labels and time series”

notes.front: What does the automatically generated up{job="...", instance="..."} time series record?
notes.back: 1 if the instance is healthy (reachable), or 0 if the scrape failed.
notes.explanation: It's stored for every instance scrape, which is what makes it useful for monitoring instance availability on its own.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Jobs and instances, “Automatically generated labels and time series”

notes.front: A team wants to alert whenever a scrape target becomes unreachable, without instrumenting anything themselves. Which automatically generated metric fits this directly?
notes.back: up — the docs describe the up time series as useful for instance availability monitoring.
notes.explanation: Because up is generated for every scrape, no extra instrumentation on the target is needed to get it.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Jobs and instances, “Automatically generated labels and time series”

notes.front: Besides scrape_configs, what are two other top-level sections a Prometheus configuration file can have?
notes.back: Any two, among others: global, rule_files, alerting, remote_write, remote_read or storage.
notes.explanation: Configuration, “Configuration file”, lays these sections out in sequence, with global providing defaults the other sections can override.

notes.front: A scrape_config for one job sets no scrape_interval of its own. Where does its effective scrape interval come from?
notes.back: The global section, which specifies parameters that are valid in all other configuration contexts and serve as their defaults.
notes.explanation: That's exactly how the docs describe the global block: defaults every scrape config falls back to unless it overrides them.

notes.front: What are Prometheus's default scrape_interval and scrape_timeout?
notes.back: scrape_interval defaults to 1 minute; scrape_timeout defaults to 10 seconds.
notes.explanation: The scrape_timeout can never be set greater than the scrape_interval, so the timeout default already fits comfortably inside the interval default.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Prometheus docs as of that date

notes.front: The default evaluation_interval — how frequently Prometheus evaluates rules — is {{c1::1 minute}}, the same default as scrape_interval.
notes.explanation: Sharing the same default value doesn't mean they're the same setting: one paces scraping, the other paces rule evaluation.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Prometheus docs as of that date

notes.front: A scrape_config sets scrape_interval to 10s and tries to set scrape_timeout to 15s. Is this a valid configuration?
notes.back: No. The docs state scrape_timeout “cannot be greater than the scrape interval.”
notes.explanation: The defaults already respect the rule: scrape_timeout defaults to 10s and scrape_interval to 1m.

notes.front: A scrape_config's metrics_path — the HTTP resource path metrics are fetched from — defaults to {{c1::/metrics}}.
notes.explanation: A target has to actually serve its metrics at that path unless the scrape_config overrides metrics_path to point somewhere else.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Prometheus docs as of that date

notes.front: An application only exposes its Prometheus metrics at /internal/metrics, not the default path. Can a scrape_config still reach it?
notes.back: Yes, by setting metrics_path to /internal/metrics in that job's scrape configuration.
notes.explanation: The default of /metrics is just that — a default — and metrics_path exists precisely so a job can point somewhere else.

notes.front: How can Prometheus be told to reload its configuration file at runtime?
notes.back: By sending a SIGHUP to the Prometheus process, or an HTTP POST request to the /-/reload endpoint.
notes.explanation: Configuration adds that the /-/reload endpoint works only when the --web.enable-lifecycle flag is enabled, and that a reload also reloads any configured rule files.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, FAQ, “Can I reload Prometheus's configuration?”

notes.front: An operator edits the configuration file with a YAML syntax error, then triggers a reload. What happens to the running configuration?
notes.back: It keeps running the old configuration. Configuration says a reload's changes are not applied if the new file is not well-formed.
notes.explanation: The FAQ puts it more loosely: Prometheus’s components “attempt to handle failing changes gracefully”.

notes.front: relabel_configs are applied to a target's label set {{c1::before it gets scraped}}, in the order they appear in the configuration file.
notes.explanation: That timing is what lets relabel_configs change which targets get scraped at all, by dropping or rewriting them beforehand.

notes.front: metric_relabel_configs are applied to samples as the {{c1::last step before ingestion}}, after the scrape has already happened.
notes.explanation: Because it runs after scraping, metric relabeling can act on the sample data itself, not just on a target's pre-scrape labels.

notes.front: What is the difference between relabel_configs and metric_relabel_configs?
notes.back: relabel_configs rewrite a target's labels before it is scraped; metric_relabel_configs rewrite samples as the last step before ingestion, after scraping.
notes.explanation: Both share the same configuration format and actions — what differs is only when, in the pipeline, each one runs.
notes.contrast: relabel_configs: pre-scrape, on targets. metric_relabel_configs: post-scrape, on samples, and it does not apply to automatically generated series such as up.

notes.front: A team writes a metric_relabel_configs rule intending to drop the up series for one job. Will this rule ever match up?
notes.back: No. Configuration says metric relabeling “does not apply to automatically generated timeseries such as up.”
notes.explanation: Metric relabeling is applied to scraped samples as the last step before ingestion; the docs give dropping series that are too expensive to ingest as one use.

notes.front: If honor_labels is set to true, how does Prometheus resolve a conflict between a scraped label and a server-side label such as job or instance?
notes.back: It keeps the label values from the scraped data and ignores the conflicting server-side labels.
notes.explanation: Configuration notes this is useful for cases like federation and scraping the Pushgateway, where the target's own labels should be preserved.

notes.front: honor_labels is set to false, and a scraped target already exposes its own "instance" label. What happens to that label?
notes.back: It's renamed to exported_instance, and Prometheus's own server-side instance label is attached instead.
notes.explanation: Configuration spells out this exact renaming pattern for false: conflicting scraped labels get an exported_ prefix.

notes.front: According to the Overview, what kind of use case is Prometheus not a good choice for?
notes.back: One needing 100% accuracy, such as per-request billing, because the collected data will likely not be detailed and complete enough.
notes.explanation: Prometheus values reliability — always being able to show what statistics are available, even under failure — over that kind of exactness.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Overview, “When does it not fit?”

notes.front: A finance team needs to charge customers per API call with no gaps or duplicates. Should this data come straight from Prometheus's scraped metrics?
notes.back: No. The Overview recommends a dedicated system for billing, and using Prometheus for the rest of the monitoring instead.
notes.explanation: Prometheus's own reliability trade-off is the reason it fits monitoring well but not exact accounting.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Overview, “When does it not fit?”

notes.front: A limitation of Prometheus's local storage is that it is {{c1::not clustered or replicated}}.
notes.explanation: That's why it “should be managed like any other single node database”, and isn't arbitrarily scalable or durable against drive or node outages on its own.

notes.front: A team asks whether local storage alone can ever hold years of Prometheus data. Does the documentation rule this out?
notes.back: No. With proper architecture, the docs say it's possible to retain years of data in local storage, even though it isn't clustered.
notes.explanation: Not being clustered limits scalability and durability, but it doesn't cap how long a single well-run node can retain data.

notes.front: How does the FAQ say Prometheus can be made highly available?
notes.back: By running identical Prometheus servers on two or more separate machines.
notes.explanation: It notes systems like Thanos, or remote write targets that support it, can then deduplicate the data those identical servers produce.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, FAQ, “Can Prometheus be made highly available?”

notes.front: A team wants Prometheus HA and assumes this means clustering several Prometheus servers into one shared storage backend. Is that what the FAQ describes?
notes.back: No. The FAQ's answer is running identical, separate servers — not a shared clustered store, which local storage doesn't provide anyway.
notes.explanation: This matches the storage page's own point: local storage is not clustered or replicated, so HA is built by duplication, not by sharing one store.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, FAQ, “Can Prometheus be made highly available?”

notes.front: In an HA setup with two identical Prometheus servers, {{c1::identical alerts}} are deduplicated by the Alertmanager.
notes.explanation: That deduplication is what stops an HA pair from paging the on-call twice for the same underlying problem.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, FAQ, “Can Prometheus be made highly available?”

notes.front: What does hierarchical federation let Prometheus scale to?
notes.back: Environments with tens of data centers and millions of nodes, with higher-level servers collecting aggregated data from many subordinate servers.
notes.explanation: The docs compare the topology to a tree: per-datacenter servers hold instance-level detail, global servers hold only aggregated, job-level data.

notes.front: A cluster scheduler's Prometheus exposes CPU and memory usage per service instance, and a service's own Prometheus wants to pull just its own service's resource figures in to query alongside its application metrics. Which kind of federation is this?
notes.back: Cross-service federation — one service's Prometheus server scraping selected data from another service's Prometheus server.
notes.explanation: This is the docs' own cluster-scheduler example: it enables alerting and queries against both datasets within a single server.
notes.contrast: Hierarchical federation: a tree of servers aggregating up, for scale. Cross-service federation: one service's server pulling in another service's selected data, for a combined view.

notes.front: If neither --storage.tsdb.retention.time nor --storage.tsdb.retention.size is set, Prometheus keeps samples for {{c1::15 days}} by default.
notes.explanation: Setting either flag changes this default: a size limit alone, for instance, removes the oldest data once that size is reached, regardless of age.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Prometheus docs as of that date

notes.front: Both --storage.tsdb.retention.time and --storage.tsdb.retention.size are set on a Prometheus server. Which one governs when data is actually removed?
notes.back: Whichever triggers first — the docs say if both time and size retention policies are specified, whichever fires first is the one applied.
notes.explanation: That makes the size limit a hard ceiling even on data that hasn't yet reached its time-based expiry, and vice versa.

notes.front: Every Prometheus time series is uniquely identified by its {{c1::metric name and optional key-value labels}}.
notes.explanation: That identity is exactly what relabeling and metric_relabel_configs can rewrite before or after a scrape, which is why changing a label can start a brand new series.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Data model, “Metric names and labels”

notes.front: A relabel_config rewrites a target's env label from "prod" to "production" before scraping. Does this change what time series the scraped samples belong to?
notes.back: Yes. Since a series is identified by its metric name and label set, changing a label's value changes which series the samples land in.
notes.explanation: This is why relabeling is powerful and risky at once: it doesn't just cosmetically rename a label, it can redirect data into a different series entirely.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Data model, “Metric names and labels”

notes.front: Label names beginning with {{c1::__ (two underscores)}} must be reserved for internal Prometheus use.
notes.explanation: Relabeling uses such labels, for example __address__ and __scheme__, and labels starting with __ are removed from the label set once target relabeling is complete.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Data model, “Metric names and labels”

notes.front: A relabel_config leaves the __meta_kubernetes_pod_name label untouched on a target. Will that label still exist once target relabeling has finished and the target gets scraped?
notes.back: No. Labels starting with __ are removed from the label set once target relabeling is complete.
notes.explanation: That's why a value worth keeping, like a meta label, has to be copied into an ordinary label first, before relabeling finishes.

notes.front: In Prometheus's own notation, how is the time series api_http_requests_total with labels method="POST" and handler="/messages" written?
notes.back: api_http_requests_total{method="POST", handler="/messages"}
notes.explanation: This <metric name>{<label name>="<label value>", ...} form is the same notation OpenTSDB uses, and it's how PromQL selectors are written too.

notes.front: Since metric names are internally represented as a label pair, a series can also be written using a special label called {{c1::__name__}}.
notes.explanation: That's why __name__ can appear directly inside a label matcher: it isn't a separate mechanism, just the metric name spelled out as a label.

notes.front: Why does the documentation say not to use a counter for the number of currently running processes?
notes.back: Because that count can decrease, and a counter's value can only increase or be reset to zero on restart.
notes.explanation: The docs give this exact example, and point to a gauge instead for anything that can go up and down.

notes.front: What's the key difference between a Prometheus counter and a gauge?
notes.back: A counter can only go up, or reset to zero on restart. A gauge can arbitrarily go up and down.
notes.explanation: Picking the wrong type doesn't just mislabel the data — PromQL functions like rate() assume counter behaviour and can give misleading results on a gauge.
notes.contrast: Counter: cumulative, monotonically increasing (e.g. requests served). Gauge: any numerical value that moves freely in either direction (e.g. current memory usage).

notes.front: A service wants to track the number of requests it is handling at this exact moment, which rises and falls as requests start and finish. Counter or gauge?
notes.back: A gauge. The docs list “the number of concurrent requests” as exactly this kind of count that can go up and down.
notes.explanation: Even though it's a count of things, what decides the metric type is whether the value can decrease, not whether it's a count.

notes.front: In the Prometheus text exposition format, how must tokens within a line be separated?
notes.back: By any number of blanks and/or tabs, with at least one whitespace character if the tokens would otherwise merge.
notes.explanation: The format is otherwise line oriented: lines are separated by a line feed, and the last line must end with one too.

notes.front: A metrics endpoint's text-format output has a blank line between two metric families. Does this break parsing?
notes.back: No. Empty lines are ignored in the Prometheus text exposition format.
notes.explanation: The same section says the format is line oriented: lines are separated by a line feed, and the last line must end with one.

notes.front: A # HELP line's remaining tokens after the metric name are treated as that metric's {{c1::docstring}}.
notes.explanation: Only one HELP line may exist for any given metric name, and it may contain any Unicode (UTF-8) characters once the backslash and line feed are escaped.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Exposition formats, “Comments, help text, and type information”

notes.front: A metric appears in a scrape with samples but no # TYPE line for it anywhere in the output. What type does Prometheus assign it?
notes.back: untyped. If there's no TYPE line for a metric name, its type is set to untyped.
notes.explanation: A TYPE line, when present, must also appear before that metric's first sample, which is why type can't be declared partway through the output.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Exposition formats, “Comments, help text, and type information”

notes.front: In the text format, each bucket count of a histogram named x is exposed as a separate sample line named {{c1::x_bucket}}, with a le label giving the bucket's upper bound.
notes.explanation: A histogram must also carry a bucket with le="+Inf", whose value must equal x_count exactly.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Exposition formats, “Histograms and summaries”

notes.front: In the text format, how is each quantile of a summary named x exposed?
notes.back: As a separate sample line with the same name x and a quantile label, such as x{quantile="0.99"}.
notes.explanation: Alongside the quantile lines, the format also expects separate x_sum and x_count lines, just as a histogram does.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Exposition formats, “Histograms and summaries”

notes.front: A histogram's text-format output lists its le="1" bucket line before its le="0.5" bucket line. Does this follow the exposition format's own convention?
notes.back: No. The format expects a histogram's buckets to appear in increasing numerical order of their le label values.
notes.explanation: The same ordering rule applies to a summary's quantile lines by their quantile label values.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Exposition formats, “Histograms and summaries”

notes.front: A monitoring config names an endpoint to scrape, but also carries the credentials and labels needed to scrape it. Is that whole bundle what Prometheus calls the target, or just the endpoint address?
notes.back: The whole bundle. A target is the definition of an object to scrape, including labels and any required authentication, not just its address.
notes.explanation: That's why a target and an instance aren't quite the same thing: instance is the resulting <host>:<port> label, while target is the fuller scrape definition behind it.

notes.front: In the docs' api-server example with four replicated instances, what single job do all four belong to?
notes.back: The api-server job — one job made up of instances 1.2.3.4:5670, 1.2.3.4:5671, 5.6.7.8:5670 and 5.6.7.8:5671.
notes.explanation: Each of the four instances is a separately scraped endpoint, but all four share the same job label because they serve the same purpose.

notes.front: Prometheus's local TSDB groups ingested samples into {{c1::two-hour}} blocks on disk.
notes.explanation: These blocks are later compacted in the background into larger blocks, up to 10% of the retention time or 31 days, whichever is smaller.

notes.front: Metric names may use any Unicode (UTF-8) character, but what does the data model say they should match for the best experience and compatibility?
notes.back: Letters, digits, underscores and colons, not starting with a digit: `[a-zA-Z_:][a-zA-Z0-9_:]*`.
notes.explanation: Names outside that recommended set need quoting, for example in PromQL, so sticking to it avoids extra friction even though it isn't mandatory.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Data model, “Metric names and labels”

notes.front: A study guide written before Prometheus 3.0 claims metric and label names must always match the classic letters/digits/underscore/colon pattern, with no exceptions. Is that still accurate?
notes.back: No. That pattern is only a recommendation now: full Unicode (UTF-8) support in metric and label names was added relatively recently, in v3.0.0.
notes.explanation: The docs still recommend sticking to that character set for the best compatibility with the wider ecosystem, even though it's no longer strictly required.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Data model, “Metric names and labels”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Prometheus docs as of that date

notes.front: A Prometheus label with an empty value is considered equivalent to a label that {{c1::does not exist}}.
notes.explanation: That's why setting a label to an empty string during relabeling has the same effect as dropping it entirely.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Data model, “Metric names and labels”

notes.front: An exporter names one of its metrics http:requests:total, using colons inside the name. Does this follow the data model's own guidance?
notes.back: No. The data model says colons are reserved for user-defined recording rules, and should not be used by exporters or direct instrumentation.
notes.explanation: Recording rules commonly use colons to separate aggregation level and operation, such as job:http_requests:rate5m, which is the naming space this reserves.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Data model, “Metric names and labels”

notes.front: A team wants to federate metrics from one Prometheus server to another using the OpenMetrics format specifically. Has this been possible since Prometheus's very first release?
notes.back: No. Exposition formats says OpenMetrics has been usable for federating metrics only since Prometheus v2.23.0.
notes.explanation: OpenMetrics itself is also comparatively recent: its inception is dated November 2020 in the docs' own basic-info table.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Exposition formats, “OpenMetrics Text Format”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Prometheus docs as of that date

notes.front: To enable exemplars, an experimental feature, Prometheus needs at least v2.26.0 and the flag {{c1::--enable-feature=exemplar-storage}}.
notes.explanation: The docs label exemplar support experimental, and it stays off until that flag is added.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Prometheus docs as of that date

notes.front: An engineer wants to eyeball a target's exposed metrics directly in a web browser to debug an issue. Should the target be negotiating the protobuf format or the text format for this?
notes.back: The text format. Exposition formats lists “not human readable” as the protobuf format's own limitation, unlike the text format's human-readable advantage.
notes.explanation: Prometheus 3.0 prefers the text-based protocols by default, and asks for protobuf first only when configured to, for example with scrape_native_histograms: true.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Exposition formats, “Prometheus Protobuf Format”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Prometheus docs as of that date

notes.front: How do the Prometheus text format, OpenMetrics and the protobuf format differ?
notes.back: Text: the human-readable default. OpenMetrics: a standardisation effort built on the text format. Protobuf: a supported binary format, not human readable.
notes.explanation: The docs list size, a strict schema and streaming among protobuf’s advantages and “not human readable” as its one limitation; the text format’s listed limitations include being verbose.
notes.contrast: Text: default, human-readable, verbose. OpenMetrics: standardised text-based format, built off the Prometheus text format. Protobuf: binary, efficient, not human-readable.

notes.front: What is the status of the Remote Write protocol's 1.0 and 2.0 specifications?
notes.back: Version 1.0 has a stable specification; version 2.0's specification is experimental. Both are supported by the Prometheus server.
notes.explanation: Only the write protocol has a stable spec at all — the corresponding remote read protocol is explicitly not yet considered a stable API.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Prometheus docs as of that date

notes.front: A team wants to build a long-term integration against Prometheus's remote read protocol and expects it to behave exactly like a stable, versioned API. Is that assumption safe?
notes.back: No. The storage docs say the remote read protocol is “not yet considered as stable API”, unlike remote write's 1.0 specification.
notes.explanation: The same page notes a separate limit: remote read only fetches raw series, and all PromQL evaluation still happens in Prometheus itself, which limits how far remote read queries scale.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Prometheus docs as of that date

notes.front: On the remote read path, all PromQL evaluation still happens in {{c1::Prometheus itself}}, not in the remote system, which is what limits its scalability.
notes.explanation: Prometheus only fetches raw series data from the remote end; fully distributed PromQL evaluation was judged infeasible for now.

notes.front: What must a request to a Prometheus server's /federate endpoint include, to select which series it returns?
notes.back: At least one match[] URL parameter, each naming an instant vector selector such as up or {job="api-server"}.
notes.explanation: If several match[] parameters are given, the endpoint returns the union of everything all of them match, not just their intersection.

notes.front: A destination server federates from a source Prometheus's /federate endpoint. Which scrape option should it enable so the source server's own labels aren't overwritten by the destination's server-side labels?
notes.back: honor_labels, set to true.
notes.explanation: Federation is one of the two cases Configuration itself names honor_labels as useful for, alongside scraping the Pushgateway.

notes.front: How do a target, a scrape and an instance relate to each other in Prometheus?
notes.back: A target is what to scrape and how. A scrape is one fetch against it. An instance is the label identifying the endpoint scraped.
notes.explanation: Confusing these is easy because the same real endpoint sits behind all three words, seen from three different angles: configuration, action and label.
notes.contrast: Target: the configured object to scrape. Scrape: the act of fetching it. Instance: the host:port label identifying it afterwards.

notes.front: A long-running web service and a short batch job both need scraping. Does the architecture diagram show Prometheus reaching both the same way?
notes.back: No. Prometheus scrapes long-running jobs directly, but reaches short-lived jobs only via an intermediary push gateway.
notes.explanation: The batch job would likely exit before a scheduled scrape could reach it, which is exactly the gap the push gateway bridges.

notes.front: A metric is named with a dot, like "http.requests", which falls outside the recommended character set. Can it still be written in Prometheus's ordinary notation without quoting?
notes.back: No. Names with characters outside the recommended set must be quoted, using the {"<metric name>", <label name>="<label value>"} form.
notes.explanation: That quoted form exists specifically for names that don't fit the plain <metric name>{...} notation.

notes.front: A team runs only one replica of a service, with no plans to scale it. Is it still meaningful to call that one replica's scrape configuration a job?
notes.back: Yes. A job is a collection of instances with the same purpose; that collection can have just one member and still be a job.
notes.explanation: Nothing in the definition requires more than one instance, only that the instances share a purpose.

notes.front: A metric http_requests_total is scraped with no method label, then later instrumentation adds method="GET" and method="POST" variants. Has the metric name changed?
notes.back: No. The metric name stays http_requests_total; only the label set changed, adding a new dimension to filter and aggregate by.
notes.explanation: This is the dimensional data model at work: labels let one metric name cover many related series, without renaming anything.
notes.source: Prometheus documentation, Data model, “Metric names and labels”

notes.front: A team wants to keep Prometheus data for years, well beyond local storage's practical retention. Which feature lets them send ingested samples to a long-term store as they arrive?
notes.back: Remote write — it sends ingested samples on the fly to other systems, such as long-term storage.
notes.explanation: This is the escape hatch for local storage's single-node limits: offloading samples elsewhere as they're ingested, rather than trying to keep everything locally.
